domain_label: Study System — Visual-Encoding & Graph-View Cartographer: Graphical Perception & Visual Encoding
purpose: A method for choosing which visual channel carries which datum in the study app's knowledge-graph and analytics views — grounding every choice in graphical-perception science (Bertin's visual variables, the Cleveland–McGill effectiveness ordering, channel-by-data-type selection) and in perceptual, colorblind-safe color so that high-yield intensity (a magnitude) rides luminance, mastery state (a category: green=known, gray=unasked, red-dot=intensity flag) rides hue plus a redundant non-color channel, and no meaning is ever carried by color alone.
assumptions: no observed dataset or user eye-tracking supplied; all scores are heuristic priors and every effectiveness-ranking claim is a domain-science ESTIMATE to source-verify in this specialist's L1 research pass

the target surfaces are a not-yet-built interactive knowledge-graph view and analytics charts; no graph library exists in the app today [FACT-source: APP_RECON §5.5], so this KB specifies the ENCODING contract those renderers must honor, not the rendering engine

the mastery-state and high-yield color scheme (green=known / gray=unasked / red-dot intensity indicator, brightness=high-yield intensity) is an owner design target from the specialist brief, not shipped code; the only shipped mastery color today is MasteryBars' green>=60/yellow>=40/red thresholding [FACT-source: APP_RECON §4c]

semantic-zoom level-of-detail, graph layout algorithms, and the specific analytics chart catalog are the OTHER two KBs of this specialist and are only referenced here where an encoding decision touches them
exclusions: semantic-zoom / cartographic level-of-detail generalization and graph layout/edge-bundling algorithms (this specialist's graph-rendering KB) beyond naming the channel budget a zoomed node can carry
the concrete analytics-chart catalog — calibration-trend and mastery-over-time chart specs (this specialist's charts KB) beyond the channel-selection rules those charts must obey

the knowledge-graph DATA and meaning layer — node/edge schema, prerequisite structure, terminology linking (the kgraph specialist) beyond consuming mastery-state and high-yield as the values to encode
the tooltip/guide explainability layer (the uxguide specialist) beyond noting that a legend is required whenever color encodes meaning
implementation-level color tokens, CSS, and the app's dark-theme palette values beyond the perceptual constraints any such palette must satisfy

competency_questions.question: What are Bertin's visual variables and why is enumerating them the first step before encoding any datum?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: names position, size, value/lightness, texture/grain, color hue, orientation and shape as the retinal variables, states each has different perceptual properties (selective/ordered/quantitative), and tags the Bertin attribution as ESTIMATE to source-verify

competency_questions.question: What is the Cleveland–McGill-tradition effectiveness ordering of encodings for reading a quantity, and how confident is it here?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: gives the ordering position/length > angle/slope > area > volume > color-saturation/density for decoding magnitude, ties it to elementary-perceptual-task accuracy, and tags it ESTIMATE to source-verify

competency_questions.question: Which channels should carry a QUANTITATIVE variable and which must be avoided?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: prescribes position/length for quantitative magnitude, allows luminance/saturation as a weaker ordered fallback, and rules out hue and shape as non-quantitative

competency_questions.question: Which channels correctly encode an ORDINAL variable such as mastery-tier or high-yield band?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: prescribes ordered channels (position, size, luminance/value, a single-hue sequential ramp) and forbids unordered channels (multi-hue, shape) for ordinal data

competency_questions.question: Which channels encode a CATEGORICAL/nominal variable such as mastery STATE, and what caps the category count?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: prescribes hue, shape and texture as selective/nominal channels, warns that discriminable categorical colors are capped at roughly a dozen, and forbids ordered channels from implying a false ranking

competency_questions.question: Why encode magnitude in a perceptual color space (CIELAB/HCL) rather than raw RGB or HSV?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: states RGB/HSV are not perceptually uniform so equal numeric steps are unequal visual steps, that perceptual spaces separate luminance from chroma/hue for even ramps, and tags the space names ESTIMATE to source-verify

competency_questions.question: What color-vision-deficiency types matter and why is a red/green mastery pair the exact hazard?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: names deutan/protan (red-green) and the rarer tritan (blue-yellow) deficiencies, notes red-green deficiency affects a substantial minority of males, and concludes a green=known/red=flag scheme is confusable without a second channel

competency_questions.question: What is redundant (double) encoding and when is it mandatory?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: defines redundant encoding as carrying one meaning on two+ channels, states it is mandatory whenever color alone would carry meaning, and gives shape/position/text/luminance as the redundant partners

competency_questions.question: How does luminance contrast make an encoding readable and colorblind-safe on the app's dark theme?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: states luminance contrast survives all color-vision deficiencies, that foreground/background contrast must clear a WCAG-style ratio, and that a dark theme constrains which hues remain distinguishable, tagging exact ratios ESTIMATE to source-verify

competency_questions.question: How is mastery state (green=known, gray=unasked, red=flag) encoded honestly and colorblind-safely?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: treats mastery state as a categorical variable on hue, requires a redundant non-color channel (shape/icon/fill pattern) because green vs red is colorblind-confusable, and keeps gray=unasked perceptually neutral/low-chroma

competency_questions.question: How is high-yield intensity encoded on brightness, and how is that kept honest?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: maps high-yield intensity (an ordered magnitude) to luminance/value along a perceptually even ramp, states brightness is an ordered but low-accuracy quantitative channel, and requires the ramp not imply finer precision than the data supports

competency_questions.question: Why is the intensity indicator a separate red DOT/badge rather than the node's hue?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: justifies a discrete red-dot mark by preattentive popout and by freeing the node's own hue for mastery state, and pairs it with a redundant cue so it is not color-only

competency_questions.question: How many independent channels can one graph node carry before the encoding is unreadable, and how do integral channels interfere?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: explains that hue and luminance on one fill are integral (they interfere), caps a node at a small number of separable channels, and resolves mastery-hue-plus-intensity-luminance by separating marks or using a border/badge

competency_questions.question: What is the recommended colorblind-safe, perceptual color-and-encoding system for the graph and charts?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: commits to mastery-state on hue+redundant shape, high-yield on luminance, red-dot as a separate double-encoded badge, perceptual palettes, luminance-contrast floors and a legend, and refuses color-only meaning and non-perceptual ramps

glossary.definition: Bertin's units of visual encoding — position, size, value/lightness, texture/grain, color hue, orientation, shape — each with distinct perceptual properties (selective, associative, ordered, quantitative) that decide which kinds of data it can honestly carry [ESTIMATE — Bertin attribution to source-verify].

The study of how accurately a human decodes a value from a visual mark; the Cleveland–McGill tradition ranks elementary perceptual tasks (position, length, angle, area, color) by decoding accuracy, and this ranking is the backbone of channel choice [ESTIMATE — to source-verify].

The approximate accuracy ranking for reading a QUANTITY: position and length are read most accurately, then angle/slope, then area, then volume, then color saturation/luminance and density least accurately — so magnitude belongs on position/length, not color [ESTIMATE — to source-verify].

Quantitative (ratio/interval magnitude), ordinal (ordered categories), and categorical/nominal (unordered labels); the datum's type dictates which visual variables are legitimate — ordered channels for ordered data, selective channels for nominal data.

Separable channels (e.g. position and hue) are read independently; integral channels (e.g. hue and luminance on one fill, or red and green light) fuse into one percept and interfere, so stacking two integral encodings on a single mark corrupts both.

A color model (CIELAB, CIELUV, HCL/LCh) built so that equal numeric distances are roughly equal perceived differences and luminance is separated from chroma and hue, unlike RGB/HSV where equal steps look uneven — required for honest sequential/diverging ramps [ESTIMATE — to source-verify].

The lightness dimension of color; an ORDERED, low-precision quantitative channel that survives every color-vision deficiency, making it the right carrier for high-yield intensity and the load-bearing channel for contrast and readability.

Reduced discrimination of certain hue pairs: deuteranomaly/deuteranopia and protanomaly/protanopia (red-green, affecting a substantial minority of males) and the rarer tritan (blue-yellow); a green-vs-red encoding is the canonical failure case [ESTIMATE — prevalence to source-verify].

Carrying a single meaning on two or more channels at once (e.g. hue AND shape, or color AND text label) so the meaning survives when one channel fails — mandatory whenever color would otherwise be the sole carrier of meaning.

The property that a mark differing on one strong channel (a saturated dot among muted nodes, a unique shape) is found in near-constant time without serial search; the basis for using a discrete red-dot badge as an attention flag rather than a subtle hue shift.

nodes.definition: Frame the problem: visual encoding is the mapping from data attributes to visual channels, and graphical perception is the science of how accurately and quickly a viewer DECODES those channels back into values. Every drawing decision in the knowledge-graph and analytics views is such a mapping, so the honest procedure is fixed here: name the datum, name its measurement type, pick the channel whose perceptual properties fit that type and whose decoding accuracy fits the required precision, then verify colorblind-safety and redundancy. The app has no graph renderer yet [FACT-source: APP_RECON §5.5], so this KB defines the encoding CONTRACT the future renderer and charts must satisfy rather than any pixels [FACT for the contract framing; the perception science it rests on is developed in later nodes and tagged there].

included: encoding as data-to-channel mapping and perception as its decoding
the name-datum / name-type / pick-channel / check-safety procedure
the contract-not-pixels role given no renderer exists yet
excluded: the specific visual variables and rankings (later nodes)
the rendering engine and layout algorithms (graph-rendering KB)

pros.claim: Framing every draw as a decodable mapping makes each color and position choice defensible against a perception criterion instead of taste
pros.example: asking 'what does this node's brightness decode to' before assigning it and rejecting a brightness that decodes to nothing

cons.claim: The frame front-loads perception theory before any pixel is drawn, which can feel heavy for a small chart
cons.example: running the full name-type-pick-check procedure for a two-series line chart that a convention would settle instantly

failure_modes: choosing a channel by aesthetics before naming the datum's type
treating encoding as styling rather than a decodable mapping
acceptance_tests: the frame states encoding as data-to-channel mapping, perception as decoding, and gives the name-datum/name-type/pick-channel/check-safety procedure with the no-renderer-yet contract role
revisit_triggers: the app adopts a specific graph library that constrains channels
a new view type is added
a downstream KB changes the encoding contract

base.update_signal: a chosen graph library or a new view type revises the encoding contract

nodes.definition: Classify every datum by measurement level before choosing a channel, because the level dictates which visual variables are legitimate. Quantitative (ratio/interval): a magnitude with meaningful distances (mastery probability 0..1, minutes studied, calibration Brier). Ordinal: ordered categories without uniform spacing (mastery tier low/medium/high, high-yield band). Categorical/nominal: unordered labels (mastery STATE known/unasked/flagged, concept FK area, exam INBDE/TOEFL). Ordered data demands an ordered channel; nominal data demands a selective channel and must NOT be put on an ordered channel that fabricates a ranking [FACT — the measurement-level-drives-channel rule is standard visualization practice; the Stevens level names are widely used, tagged ESTIMATE only for exact historical attribution]. This taxonomy is the switch every channel-selection node reads.

included: quantitative vs ordinal vs categorical/nominal definitions
worked classification of the app's own values
the ordered-data-needs-ordered-channel / nominal-data-needs-selective-channel rule
excluded: the channel prescriptions themselves (their own nodes)
the color-space mechanics

pros.claim: Fixing the measurement level first prevents the most common encoding error: an ordered channel on nominal data implying a false ranking
pros.example: refusing to put mastery STATE on a brightness ramp that would rank 'unasked' as more-than or less-than 'known'

cons.claim: Some app values are genuinely ambiguous between ordinal and quantitative, so the classification is a judgment that can be revised
cons.example: high-yield 'intensity' treated as a smooth magnitude by one view and as three bands by another

failure_modes: encoding nominal categories on an ordered channel and fabricating a ranking
treating an ordinal band as continuous and overstating precision
acceptance_tests: the three measurement levels are defined, the app's values are each classified, and the ordered-vs-selective channel rule is stated
revisit_triggers: a value's measurement level is reinterpreted
a new data attribute enters a view
a downstream encoding implies the wrong level

base.update_signal: a reinterpreted measurement level or a new attribute changes the classification

nodes.definition: Enumerate the visual variables — the toolkit from which every encoding is drawn. Bertin's retinal variables are position (planar x,y), size, value/lightness, texture/grain, color hue, orientation, and shape [ESTIMATE — to source-verify: attributed to Bertin's Semiology of Graphics, exact list and edition to confirm in L1 research]. Each has different perceptual PROPERTIES: position and size are quantitative and ordered; value/lightness is ordered but not quantitative; hue and shape are selective (good for telling categories apart) but NOT ordered; texture and orientation are weaker. The property, not the variable's familiarity, decides its legitimate use — this is why hue can label a category but must never carry a magnitude, and why lightness can carry an ordered intensity but reads only coarsely.

included: the roster of visual variables
each variable's perceptual property (ordered / selective / quantitative)
the property-decides-use principle
excluded: the accuracy RANKING among quantitative encodings (its own node)
color-space internals

pros.claim: Naming the variables and their properties gives an exhaustive, principled palette so no channel is used against its nature
pros.example: picking lightness for an ordered intensity and hue for an unordered state because their properties say so

cons.claim: The classic list predates modern displays and interaction, so motion, blur and opacity are additional channels it omits
cons.example: using opacity or a subtle animation as an encoding the seven-variable list does not enumerate

failure_modes: using a selective variable (hue) to carry a magnitude
treating all variables as interchangeable ignoring their properties
acceptance_tests: the visual variables are listed with each one's perceptual property and the property-decides-use principle, with the Bertin attribution tagged ESTIMATE to source-verify
revisit_triggers: modern channels (opacity, motion) must be added
an L1 source revises the canonical list
a variable is used against its property

base.update_signal: an L1 source verification or added modern channels revise the variable roster

nodes.definition: Order the quantitative encodings by decoding accuracy, the Cleveland–McGill-tradition result: for reading a MAGNITUDE, position along a common scale and length are decoded most accurately, then angle/slope, then area, then volume, then color saturation/luminance and density least accurately [ESTIMATE — to source-verify: the Cleveland & McGill elementary-perceptual-task ranking, exact 1984-tradition ordering to confirm in L1 research]. The rule that falls out: put the value the user must read PRECISELY on position or length, and accept color/area only for values that may be read approximately. This ranking is why a bar or dot-plot beats a color heat-map for exact comparison, and why encoding high-yield intensity on brightness is legitimate only because intensity is a coarse, ordered signal, not a number to be read off.

included: the accuracy ordering position/length > angle > area > volume > color/density
the precise-value-on-position, approximate-value-on-color rule
why heat-maps lose to bars for exact reads
excluded: per-data-type channel prescriptions (their own nodes)
colorblind considerations

pros.claim: A single accuracy ordering settles most channel disputes by matching required precision to the channel that supports it
pros.example: choosing a dot-plot over a color grid when the user must rank concepts by mastery exactly

cons.claim: The ranking is for reading a single value; it under-weights that color enables fast gestalt scanning of many marks at once
cons.example: a mastery heat-map read worse per-cell but far faster overall than a hundred separate bars

failure_modes: putting a must-be-precise value on a low-accuracy color channel
citing the ranking as fact without the source-verify tag
acceptance_tests: the accuracy ordering is stated, the precise-on-position vs approximate-on-color rule is derived, and the ranking is tagged ESTIMATE to source-verify
revisit_triggers: an L1 source refines the ordering
a gestalt/scanning task outweighs single-value accuracy
a new channel must be placed in the ranking

base.update_signal: an L1 source verification or a scanning-task priority changes the ranking's use

nodes.definition: Establish preattentive popout: a mark that differs from its neighbors on one strong channel — a saturated dot among muted nodes, a unique shape, high luminance contrast — is located in near-constant time without serial search, whereas a target defined by a CONJUNCTION of channels forces slow serial search [ESTIMATE — to source-verify: preattentive-feature findings from the visual-search literature, exact studies to confirm in L1 research]. The design consequences: reserve a high-salience channel for the ONE thing the user must not miss (the red-dot high-priority flag), keep the graph's default nodes low-salience so a flag can pop, and never require the user to find a target by combining two subtle channels. Popout is a scarce resource — over-using saturation everywhere destroys it.

included: single-feature popout vs slow conjunction search
reserving salience for the must-not-miss flag
keeping defaults low-salience so flags pop
excluded: the red-dot indicator's full spec (its own node)
the effectiveness ranking for quantitative reads

pros.claim: Spending salience on exactly one flag makes urgent items findable at a glance across a dense graph
pros.example: a single red high-priority dot located instantly among dozens of neutral nodes

cons.claim: Salience is zero-sum, so every extra emphasized element erodes popout and the view degrades to uniform noise
cons.example: coloring half the nodes brightly so no single flag stands out any more

failure_modes: requiring a conjunction search to find an important node
over-saturating the default view so nothing pops
acceptance_tests: popout is defined against conjunction search, salience is reserved for the single flag, and defaults are kept low-salience, tagged ESTIMATE to source-verify
revisit_triggers: multiple competing flags appear
the default node styling grows too salient
an L1 source revises the preattentive set

base.update_signal: competing flags or an L1 source change revise the salience budget

nodes.definition: Distinguish separable from integral channels, the constraint on stacking encodings. Separable channels (position and hue, size and shape) are attended independently, so two data attributes on them are read without interference. Integral channels fuse into a single percept — hue and luminance applied to the same fill, or red and green light, cannot be judged independently and their combination reads as one blended color [ESTIMATE — to source-verify: separable/integral-dimension findings, exact sources to confirm in L1 research]. Consequence for the graph node: mastery on hue AND high-yield intensity on the SAME fill's luminance are integral and will corrupt each other; two attributes may share a mark only if carried on separable channels (e.g. fill hue plus border thickness, or fill plus a detached badge). This is the hard limit the multi-channel-node node builds on.

included: separable vs integral channel definitions
hue+luminance-on-one-fill as the integral hazard
the rule that shared marks need separable channels
excluded: the per-node channel budget count (its own node)
the colorblind mechanics

pros.claim: Knowing which channel pairs interfere prevents silently corrupting two encodings that share a mark
pros.example: moving high-yield intensity to a border because it would blend with mastery hue if both sat on the fill

cons.claim: Integral pairs can be exploited deliberately for a single blended judgment, so the rule is a caution not an absolute ban
cons.example: a bivariate choropleth that intentionally blends two hues where a single combined read is wanted

failure_modes: stacking hue and luminance on one fill and blending two meanings into noise
assuming all channel pairs are independent
acceptance_tests: separable and integral channels are defined, hue+luminance-on-one-fill is named the hazard, and the separable-channels-for-shared-marks rule is stated
revisit_triggers: a bivariate blended encoding is intentionally wanted
a new channel pair's interference is uncertain
the node gains another attribute

base.update_signal: an intentional bivariate blend or an L1 source change revises the interference rule

nodes.definition: Prescribe channels for QUANTITATIVE data. Because position and length top the accuracy ranking, a magnitude the user must read or compare precisely — mastery probability, minutes studied, calibration error over time — belongs on position along a common scale (bar height, dot position, line y-value). Size/area is an acceptable second choice for approximate magnitude but is decoded with systematic underestimation of large values, so avoid area for precise comparison. Luminance/saturation is an ORDERED but low-accuracy quantitative fallback, legitimate only when the value may be read coarsely (a heat-map for scanning, high-yield intensity). Hue and shape are NOT quantitative and must never carry a magnitude [derived from GRAPHICAL_PERCEPTION_RANKING; FACT that hue is non-quantitative, the accuracy ordering itself tagged ESTIMATE in its own node].

included: position/length as the precise-quantitative channels
area as approximate-only with underestimation caveat
luminance/saturation as a coarse ordered fallback and hue/shape as forbidden for magnitude
excluded: ordinal and categorical prescriptions (their own nodes)
the color-space that makes a luminance ramp even

pros.claim: Routing precise magnitudes to position/length makes the analytics charts read accurately by construction
pros.example: a calibration-trend line and a mastery bar chart instead of a color grid when exact values matter

cons.claim: Position is expensive in screen space, so a dense graph cannot give every node its own axis and must fall back to weaker channels
cons.example: hundreds of concept nodes that cannot each occupy a common scale and must use size or color instead

failure_modes: encoding a must-compare value on hue or area
using position where space forbids it and crowding the view
acceptance_tests: position/length are prescribed for precise magnitude, area is flagged approximate-with-underestimation, luminance is allowed as a coarse fallback, and hue/shape are forbidden for magnitude
revisit_triggers: screen-space limits force a weaker channel
a value's required precision changes

base.update_signal: a space constraint or a precision-requirement change alters the channel choice

nodes.definition: Prescribe channels for ORDINAL data — ordered categories without uniform spacing, such as a mastery tier (low/medium/high) or a high-yield band. Ordinal data needs an ORDERED channel that shows rank without implying exact ratios: position, size, luminance/value, or a single-hue SEQUENTIAL ramp (light-to-dark of one hue). It must NOT go on an unordered channel — a multi-hue categorical palette or shape — because those hide the ordering, nor should it be drawn so smoothly that it reads as continuous quantitative data it is not [FACT — ordered-data-needs-ordered-channel is standard practice; rests on the visual-variable properties]. High-yield intensity, treated as an ordered band, is the app's central ordinal case and rides luminance for exactly this reason.

included: ordered channels for ordinal data (position, size, luminance, single-hue sequential ramp)
the ban on multi-hue/shape for ordered data
not over-smoothing an ordinal band into false continuity
excluded: the quantitative and categorical prescriptions
the perceptual-uniformity mechanics of the ramp

pros.claim: A single-hue luminance ramp shows rank at a glance without fabricating exact ratios the data lack
pros.example: three high-yield bands as three luminance steps that read as ordered but not as precise numbers

cons.claim: Ordinal-on-luminance shares the low accuracy of all color channels, so fine rank distinctions blur
cons.example: five ordinal bands on luminance where adjacent steps become hard to tell apart

failure_modes: putting ordered bands on a multi-hue palette that hides the order
rendering discrete bands as a smooth gradient implying continuity
acceptance_tests: ordered channels are prescribed for ordinal data, multi-hue/shape are forbidden, and over-smoothing into false continuity is warned against
revisit_triggers: the number of ordinal bands grows beyond luminance's resolution
an ordinal value is reclassified as quantitative
a ramp is misread as continuous

base.update_signal: more bands than luminance resolves or a reclassification changes the ordinal channel

nodes.definition: Prescribe channels for CATEGORICAL/nominal data — unordered labels such as mastery STATE (known/unasked/flagged), concept FK area, or exam code. Nominal data needs a SELECTIVE channel that lets the eye group like with like without implying rank: hue (a qualitative palette of distinct hues), shape, or texture. Two hard limits: the number of reliably discriminable categorical colors is small — on the order of a dozen at most, fewer on a busy background — so high-cardinality categories must group, facet, or use position instead; and a nominal variable must NEVER ride an ordered channel (luminance ramp) that would fabricate a ranking among unordered labels [FACT — the selective-channel rule and the ~dozen-color limit are standard practice; the exact count tagged ESTIMATE]. Mastery state is the app's primary categorical encoding and is developed in its own node.

included: hue/shape/texture as selective nominal channels
the ~dozen discriminable categorical colors limit
the ban on ordered channels for nominal data
excluded: the mastery-state encoding specifics (its own node)
the colorblind-safety mechanics

pros.claim: Selective channels let a viewer instantly pick out all nodes of one category without reading a legend for each
pros.example: all 'unasked' nodes recognizable as one group by a shared neutral treatment

cons.claim: Categorical color capacity is tiny, so any scheme with many categories overruns discriminability and needs grouping or faceting
cons.example: ten INBDE FK areas plus mastery states exceeding the dozen-color budget on one graph

failure_modes: assigning more categorical colors than are discriminable
putting nominal labels on a luminance ramp implying rank
acceptance_tests: hue/shape/texture are prescribed for nominal data, the ~dozen-color limit is stated as ESTIMATE, and ordered channels are forbidden for nominal data
revisit_triggers: category count exceeds the discriminable-color budget

base.update_signal: an over-budget category count or a false-ranking misuse changes the categorical channel

nodes.definition: Require a perceptual color space for any color that encodes data. RGB and HSV are device/convenience spaces that are NOT perceptually uniform: equal numeric steps produce visually uneven jumps, and HSV's 'value' mixes luminance with hue so a yellow and a blue at the same HSV value differ greatly in apparent lightness. Perceptual spaces — CIELAB, CIELUV, HCL/LCh — are built so equal distances are roughly equal perceived differences and, crucially, separate LUMINANCE from chroma and hue, which is what lets a sequential ramp step evenly and lets luminance be controlled independently for contrast [ESTIMATE — to source-verify: the space names and their uniformity properties, exact references to confirm in L1 research]. Every ramp and palette in this KB is specified in a perceptual space, then converted to the app's output color at render time.

included: why RGB/HSV are non-uniform and mix luminance with hue
perceptual spaces (CIELAB/HCL) and luminance separation
specifying ramps in a perceptual space then converting at render
excluded: the specific sequential/diverging palettes (their own node)
the accessibility contrast thresholds

pros.claim: Specifying color in a perceptual space makes ramps step evenly and lets luminance be tuned for contrast without shifting hue
pros.example: a mastery ramp whose visual steps are equal instead of bunching in the greens as an HSV ramp would

cons.claim: Perceptual-space math and gamut clipping add conversion complexity over picking hex values directly
cons.example: an HCL color that falls outside the display gamut and must be clipped, subtly breaking uniformity

failure_modes: building a magnitude ramp in RGB/HSV so steps look uneven
assuming equal HSV value means equal apparent lightness
acceptance_tests: RGB/HSV non-uniformity and luminance-mixing are stated, perceptual spaces with luminance separation are required, and the space names are tagged ESTIMATE to source-verify
revisit_triggers: an L1 source pins the exact space to use
gamut clipping distorts a ramp

base.update_signal: an L1 source pin or a gamut/pipeline change revises the color space

nodes.definition: Characterize luminance (lightness/value) as its own load-bearing channel. Luminance is ORDERED — lighter reads as more or less along a scale — making it a legitimate ordinal/coarse-quantitative carrier; it is LOW precision, so only a handful of steps are reliably distinguished; and it is the ONE color dimension that survives every color-vision deficiency, so it doubles as the channel for contrast and readability [FACT — luminance is ordered and CVD-robust; the exact number of distinguishable steps tagged ESTIMATE]. This triple role is why the KB assigns high-yield INTENSITY to luminance (ordered magnitude) while also reserving luminance headroom for text/edge contrast — the two uses compete for the same finite dynamic range and must be budgeted together, especially on the app's dark theme where the usable luminance range is compressed.

included: luminance as ordered, low-precision, CVD-robust
its triple role (intensity encoding, contrast, readability)
the finite-dynamic-range budgeting, tighter on a dark theme
excluded: the specific WCAG contrast ratios (accessibility node)
the high-yield intensity mapping specifics (its own node)

pros.claim: Using luminance for the ordered intensity keeps that encoding readable by colorblind users for free
pros.example: high-yield brightness that a deutan user still reads as ordered because it is luminance not hue

cons.claim: Luminance is a single finite range shared by intensity and contrast, so spending it on encoding can starve readability
cons.example: a bright high-yield node whose text label loses contrast against its own light fill

failure_modes: encoding many intensity steps on luminance beyond what is distinguishable
using up luminance on encoding and leaving text under-contrasted
acceptance_tests: luminance is characterized as ordered, low-precision and CVD-robust, its triple role is stated, and the shared-dynamic-range budget under the dark theme is noted
revisit_triggers: the theme's luminance range changes
intensity needs more steps than luminance resolves
text contrast fails over an encoded fill

base.update_signal: a theme range change or a contrast failure re-budgets the luminance channel

nodes.definition: Match palette TYPE to data type, the color analogue of channel selection. Sequential palettes (one hue, light-to-dark) encode ordered/quantitative data by luminance and are correct for high-yield intensity and mastery magnitude. Diverging palettes (two hues meeting at a neutral midpoint) encode data with a meaningful center — calibration over/under a target, mastery above/below a threshold — and are wrong for data without a natural midpoint. Qualitative/categorical palettes (distinct hues at similar luminance) encode nominal categories and must NOT be used for ordered data because their equal luminance hides rank [FACT — the sequential/diverging/qualitative-to-data-type mapping is standard practice]. Choosing the wrong palette family is a common, high-impact error: a rainbow (multi-hue) ramp on quantitative data both misleads on order and fails colorblind users.

included: sequential/diverging/qualitative palette families and their matching data types
diverging only for centered data
why a rainbow ramp on quantitative data is wrong
excluded: the colorblind-safe hue selection (accessibility nodes)

nodes.definition: Make color encodings robust to color-vision deficiency. The common deficiencies are deuteranomaly/deuteranopia and protanomaly/protanopia (red-green confusion, affecting a substantial minority of males and far fewer females) and the rarer tritan (blue-yellow); together they mean a design must not rely on any single hue pair being distinguishable [FACT — red-green is the dominant CVD; exact prevalence figures tagged ESTIMATE to source-verify]. The two robust levers are: separate colors by LUMINANCE (which all CVD types retain) rather than by hue alone, and choose CVD-safe hue families (blue/orange rather than red/green) — but even a safe palette is verified by simulating each deficiency, not assumed. Because the app's mastery scheme is literally green-versus-red, this node is a hard constraint on the mastery-state encoding, forcing a redundant non-color channel.

included: deutan/protan (red-green) and tritan (blue-yellow) deficiencies
separate-by-luminance and CVD-safe hue families as the levers
simulate-to-verify and the green-vs-red hazard for mastery
excluded: the redundant-encoding mechanism (its own node)
the WCAG contrast ratios

pros.claim: Designing for CVD from the start makes the encoding legible to every user rather than a majority
pros.example: a mastery scheme a red-green-deficient user still reads because state also differs in shape and luminance

cons.claim: CVD-safe hue families shrink the usable palette and can clash with brand/convention (green=good, red=bad)
cons.example: abandoning the intuitive red/green semantics to stay safe, then having to re-teach the meaning

assuming a palette is safe without simulating each deficiency

nodes.definition: Establish redundant (double) encoding: carry one meaning on two or more channels at once so the meaning survives any single channel failing. The rule is unconditional — whenever color would be the SOLE carrier of a distinction, add a second channel: shape/icon, position, a text label, a fill pattern, or a luminance difference [FACT — redundant encoding for color-independence is standard accessibility practice; rests on the CVD and separable-channel nodes]. Redundancy is not clutter when the channels are separable and reinforce the same grouping; it becomes clutter only when a second channel encodes a DIFFERENT variable and competes. For the app this means mastery state is hue PLUS a shape/icon, the red-dot flag is color PLUS a distinct badge position, and any chart series distinguished by color also differs in marker or dash. Redundancy is also what lets the design degrade gracefully in grayscale print or on a failing display.

included: carrying one meaning on 2+ channels
the unconditional rule when color would be sole carrier
the shape/position/text/pattern/luminance partners and the not-clutter caveat
excluded: the specific mastery/red-dot encodings (their own nodes)
the contrast-ratio floors

pros.claim: Doubling color with a non-color channel makes every distinction survive colorblindness, grayscale and glare at once

cons.claim: Redundancy consumes channels that could carry more data, so on a dense node it competes with encoding additional attributes

nodes.definition: Set the luminance-contrast floor that makes every mark readable and CVD-robust. Because luminance contrast survives all color-vision deficiencies and drives legibility, foreground marks and text must clear a minimum contrast ratio against their background, and adjacent encoded regions must differ enough in luminance to be told apart independent of hue [FACT — luminance contrast is the CVD-robust readability channel; the specific WCAG ratios (on the order of 4.5:1 for text, 3:1 for large text/graphics) tagged ESTIMATE to source-verify]. The dark theme both helps (bright marks pop on a dark ground) and constrains (the usable light-to-dark range is compressed and some dark hues collapse toward the background). This node supplies the contrast constraint the mastery, intensity and red-dot encodings must each pass, and it competes with intensity for the same luminance range.

included: a minimum foreground/background contrast ratio
adjacent-region luminance separation independent of hue
the dark-theme help-and-constraint on the usable range
excluded: the exact certified WCAG numbers (source-verify in L1)
the intensity mapping that consumes the same range

pros.claim: A luminance-contrast floor guarantees readability for every user and every CVD type in one testable rule
pros.example: a contrast check that a mastery color must pass against the dark background before it ships

cons.claim: A hard contrast floor restricts the palette, ruling out subtle dark-on-dark encodings the designer might want

nodes.definition: Encode mastery STATE — the owner's green=known, gray=unasked, red=needs-attention scheme — as a CATEGORICAL variable done safely. State is nominal (three unordered labels), so hue is the natural selective channel, BUT green-versus-red is exactly the red-green CVD confusion, so hue alone is forbidden: each state carries a REDUNDANT non-color cue (a distinct node shape or icon — e.g. filled check for known, hollow ring for unasked, alert glyph for flagged) and the states are separated in LUMINANCE as well as hue [FACT-source: the green/gray/red scheme is an owner design target in SPECIALIST_LIST §C2; FACT that green-vs-red is CVD-confusable per COLORBLIND_SAFETY; the shipped app today only thresholds MasteryBars green/yellow/red per APP_RECON §4c, so this graph-node scheme is a design target not shipped code]. Gray=unasked is kept low-chroma and mid-low luminance so it reads as neutral/absent, never as a fourth color competing with the two meaningful states.

gray=unasked as low-chroma neutral
the green-vs-red CVD hazard forcing redundancy
excluded: the high-yield intensity encoding (its own node)
the red-dot flag mark (its own node)

pros.example: a colorblind user reading 'known' from a check icon and higher luminance even if green and red look alike

cons.example: three distinct node glyphs cluttering a dense graph where a single dot would be calmer

letting gray-unasked gain chroma and read as a third meaningful color

nodes.definition: Encode high-yield INTENSITY on luminance/brightness. High-yield intensity is an ordered magnitude (how important a concept is to the exam), so it rides the ordered luminance channel along a single-hue SEQUENTIAL ramp built in a perceptual space: brighter = higher yield, stepping perceptually evenly [FACT that intensity is ordered and belongs on an ordered channel; the specific brightness=high-yield mapping is an owner design target from SPECIALIST_LIST §C2, not shipped]. Two disciplines keep it honest: luminance is low precision, so the ramp exposes only a few bands (say three to five), never a false continuum implying the underlying yield score is known to the decimal; and because intensity SHARES the luminance channel with mastery-state luminance separation and with contrast, the three uses are budgeted together so a very-high-yield bright node still clears text contrast and does not collide with a 'known' state that is also lighter. Intensity on luminance also inherits colorblind-safety for free.

included: high-yield intensity as ordered magnitude on a single-hue luminance ramp
few-band quantization to avoid false precision
budgeting the shared luminance range against state and contrast
excluded: the honesty/abstraction principle in general (its own node)
the multi-channel interference resolution (its own node)

pros.claim: Putting intensity on luminance makes it an ordered, colorblind-safe signal readable at a glance across the graph
pros.example: the brightest nodes reading as highest-yield to every user without a legend lookup

cons.claim: Luminance is shared and low precision, so intensity gets only a few honest bands and competes with state and contrast for range
cons.example: a bright high-yield node clashing with a bright 'known' node when both push luminance up

failure_modes: rendering intensity as a smooth ramp implying decimal precision the yield score lacks

nodes.definition: Specify the red-dot intensity/attention indicator as a SEPARATE discrete mark, not the node's own hue. Making the flag a detached badge (a small saturated dot at a fixed node corner) exploits preattentive popout so an urgent item is found in near-constant time, AND frees the node's fill hue to carry mastery state and its luminance to carry high-yield intensity without collision [FACT that a discrete high-salience mark pops preattentively per PREATTENTIVE_POPOUT; the red-dot indicator is an owner design target from SPECIALIST_LIST §C2]. Because red alone is CVD-risky and popout must not be color-only, the dot is redundantly encoded by its distinct SHAPE and fixed POSITION (a mark that is present-or-absent at a known spot), so a colorblind user detects the badge by its presence and placement, not its redness. Salience discipline applies: the dot is reserved for the single highest-priority signal, or it stops popping.

included: the flag as a separate popout badge freeing node hue/luminance
redundant encoding by shape and fixed position, not redness
salience discipline reserving it for the top signal
excluded: what condition triggers the flag (kgraph/learner data)
the node's own state and intensity encodings

pros.claim: A detached popout badge makes urgent nodes findable instantly while leaving the node's own channels free for state and intensity
pros.example: a red dot located at a glance across a dense graph without disturbing the node's mastery color

cons.claim: A badge adds a mark to already busy nodes and, if over-applied, destroys the popout it depends on

failure_modes: encoding the flag as the node's hue and colliding with mastery state
relying on redness alone so colorblind users miss the flag
over-applying the dot until popout is lost
acceptance_tests: the indicator is a separate popout badge that frees node hue/luminance, is redundantly encoded by shape and fixed position rather than redness, and is reserved for the single top-priority signal, with the design-target source

nodes.definition: Compose the three node encodings without interference. A single graph node must carry mastery state, high-yield intensity, and possibly a red-dot flag; the separable/integral rule governs whether they can coexist. Mastery HUE and intensity LUMINANCE on the same fill are INTEGRAL and would blend, so the composition separates them across marks: assign one attribute to the fill and route the second to a SEPARABLE carrier — a border/ring (hue or thickness), a detached badge, or the node's size — and keep the redundant state shape as a fourth, low-cost cue [FACT — the integral-hue-luminance hazard and the separable-carrier fix rest on SEPARABLE_INTEGRAL_CHANNELS]. The safe default: fill LUMINANCE = intensity, fill HUE constrained to the mastery family, state redundancy on SHAPE, flag on a detached DOT — a layout where each meaning lands on a channel the others do not touch, verified by simulating that removing any one channel leaves the others intact.

included: separating integral hue+luminance across fill and a separable carrier
the safe default channel assignment for a node
verify-by-removal that channels do not interfere
excluded: the total channel-count budget (its own node)
the individual encodings' internals

pros.claim: Routing each meaning to a channel the others do not touch lets one node honestly carry state, intensity and a flag at once
pros.example: a node whose luminance reads intensity, ring reads state and badge reads a flag, each independently

nodes.definition: Enforce honesty in the encoding itself: a mark must not imply more precision, certainty, or structure than the data support. Because color and area are LOW-accuracy channels, encoding a value on them and then inviting exact reads is dishonest; and rendering a coarse, uncertain, or banded quantity (a high-yield score, a mastery estimate with wide uncertainty) as a smooth continuous ramp fabricates precision [FACT — the low-accuracy-of-color premise rests on GRAPHICAL_PERCEPTION_RANKING; the honesty mandate mirrors the specialist's house honesty contract]. The disciplines: quantize low-confidence magnitudes into a few bands, show uncertainty explicitly (a muted or hatched treatment for low-evidence estimates) rather than a confident solid color, and reserve high-accuracy channels (position/length in the charts) for the values that are actually known precisely. This is the visual analogue of the FACT/ESTIMATE/UNKNOWN tagging: the picture must not over-claim.

included: not implying precision/certainty beyond the data
quantizing low-confidence magnitudes and showing uncertainty explicitly
reserving high-accuracy channels for precisely-known values
excluded: semantic-zoom abstraction of the graph (graph-rendering KB)
the specific uncertainty source (learner model)

pros.claim: Encoding uncertainty and banding coarse values keeps the visualization from over-claiming what the models actually know
pros.example: a low-evidence mastery node shown muted/hatched rather than a confident solid green

cons.claim: Honest uncertainty treatments add visual complexity and can look less polished than a clean confident fill
cons.example: hatched low-confidence nodes making the graph busier than a uniform color would

failure_modes: rendering an uncertain estimate as a confident smooth color
inviting exact reads off a low-accuracy color channel
acceptance_tests: the encoding avoids implying unsupported precision, quantizes low-confidence magnitudes, shows uncertainty explicitly, and reserves high-accuracy channels for precisely-known values
revisit_triggers: a value's confidence changes

base.update_signal: a confidence change or observed false-precision reads tighten the honesty rule

nodes.definition: Bound the total number of simultaneous encodings a single view or node can carry before it becomes unreadable. Each additional attribute consumes a separable channel, and viewers reliably attend only a few at once, so a node should carry a small number of independent meanings — as a working cap, on the order of three to four (e.g. state, intensity, flag, plus label) — beyond which additional channels interfere or are ignored [ESTIMATE, medium confidence — the small-capacity limit is well established in the attention literature; the exact number to source-verify in L1]. The budget interacts with semantic zoom (handled by the graph-rendering KB): zoomed OUT, drop to the one or two channels that survive at small size (position and a single color) and show concise names; zoomed IN, spend the fuller budget. When the budget is exceeded, the resolution is to remove, aggregate, or move a channel into interaction (hover/detail), never to cram.

shedding channels when zoomed out and spending them zoomed in

cons.example: an expert-facing detail view legibly carrying more channels than the default cap suggests

failure_modes: encoding more attributes than viewers can attend

acceptance_tests: a small-number channel cap is stated as ESTIMATE, channel-shedding on zoom-out is prescribed, and overload is resolved by remove/aggregate/move-to-interaction
revisit_triggers: a view needs more channels than the cap

nodes.definition: Compose the recommended encoding-and-color system the KB builds toward. GO: mastery STATE on a CVD-safe hue family PLUS a redundant shape/icon and luminance separation (green=known, gray=unasked low-chroma neutral, flag family), high-yield INTENSITY on a single-hue perceptual luminance ramp quantized to a few honest bands, the attention flag as a SEPARATE popout red DOT double-encoded by shape and fixed position, all palettes built in a perceptual space, every color meaning backed by a legend and a luminance-contrast floor, and a per-node channel budget with channels shed on zoom-out [synthesis over the prior nodes; the app color scheme is an owner design target per SPECIALIST_LIST §C2, the shipped baseline is MasteryBars per APP_RECON §4c, and no graph renderer exists yet per APP_RECON §5.5]. edge_cases.description: On the dark theme a low-mastery dark node collapses into the background
edge_cases.trigger: an encoded dark hue has too little luminance contrast with the dark ground
edge_cases.mitigation: raise the node's minimum luminance or add a border so even the darkest state stays visible

edge_cases.description: Zoomed all the way out, fully-encoded nodes turn to indistinct mud
edge_cases.trigger: the full channel budget is kept at small render sizes
edge_cases.mitigation: shed to position plus one color and concise names when zoomed out, restoring channels on zoom-in

edge_cases.description: A palette assumed safe fails for a specific deficiency
edge_cases.trigger: a color pair is adopted without simulating each CVD type
edge_cases.mitigation: simulate deutan, protan and tritan on every palette before shipping and revise any confused pair

workflow.action: Frame the encoding as a decodable mapping and classify the datum
workflow.description: State the name-datum/name-type/pick-channel/check-safety procedure and classify each value as quantitative, ordinal or categorical
workflow.gate: every value to be drawn is classified by measurement level before any channel is chosen

workflow.action: Enumerate the visual variables and their perceptual properties
workflow.description: List position/size/value/texture/hue/orientation/shape with each one's ordered/selective/quantitative property
workflow.gate: each variable is listed with its property and the Bertin attribution is tagged ESTIMATE to source-verify

workflow.description: Order encodings by decoding accuracy and derive precise-on-position, approximate-on-color
workflow.gate: the ordering is stated, the precise-vs-approximate rule derived, and the ranking tagged ESTIMATE to source-verify

workflow.description: Give the quantitative, ordinal and categorical channel choices and their forbidden channels
workflow.gate: quantitative→position/length, ordinal→ordered channels, categorical→selective channels are prescribed with the forbidden channels named

workflow.action: Specify perceptual color and palette families
workflow.description: Require a perceptual space, characterize luminance, and match sequential/diverging/qualitative palettes to data types
workflow.gate: RGB/HSV non-uniformity is stated, a perceptual space is required, and palette families are matched to data types

workflow.action: Impose colorblind-safety, redundancy and contrast floors
workflow.description: Name CVD types, require separate-by-luminance and redundant encoding, and set a luminance-contrast floor
workflow.gate: CVD types are named, redundant encoding is mandated where color would be sole carrier, and a contrast floor is set

workflow.description: Encode green/gray/red state on hue plus a redundant shape and luminance separation with gray as neutral
workflow.gate: state is nominal on hue PLUS a redundant shape with luminance separation, gray=unasked kept neutral, sources cited

workflow.action: Encode high-yield intensity and keep it honest
workflow.description: Map intensity to a quantized perceptual luminance ramp and show uncertainty rather than false precision
workflow.gate: intensity rides a single-hue luminance ramp quantized to a few bands with uncertainty shown, not a false continuum

workflow.action: Add the red-dot flag as a separate popout badge
workflow.description: Make the flag a detached shape-and-position badge reserved for the top signal, freeing node hue/luminance
workflow.gate: the flag is a separate popout badge double-encoded by shape and position and reserved for one top-priority condition

workflow.description: Assign state, intensity and flag to separable non-interfering channels and cap the total per node
workflow.gate: integral hue+luminance are separated across fill and a carrier, and the node stays within the channel budget verified by removal

workflow.action: Compose and stress-test the color-system verdict
workflow.description: State the go system and no-go list and run CVD simulation and contrast checks over the whole scheme
workflow.gate: the go/no-go verdict is stated and the scheme passes CVD simulation, contrast floors and the channel budget

dominance_rules.rule: The datum's measurement level dominates the designer's channel preference
dominance_rules.rationale: a channel used against the data type fabricates order or hides it, misleading regardless of intent
dominance_rules.trigger: a channel is chosen before the data type is fixed
dominance_rules.action: classify the value first and pick only a channel whose property fits that level

dominance_rules.rationale: an encoding a substantial minority cannot read is broken however intuitive its hues are to others
dominance_rules.trigger: a meaning would rest on a red-green (or other confusable) hue distinction
dominance_rules.action: add a redundant non-color channel and separate by luminance, then verify by CVD simulation

dominance_rules.rule: Luminance contrast dominates intensity resolution when they collide
dominance_rules.rationale: an unreadable mark conveys nothing, so readability outranks squeezing more intensity bands from the range
dominance_rules.trigger: an intensity value pushes luminance past the contrast floor
dominance_rules.action: cap the intensity ramp or re-contrast the label so the contrast floor always holds

dominance_rules.rule: Separable-channel placement dominates compact single-fill packing
dominance_rules.rationale: two integral encodings on one fill blend into an unreadable color, losing both meanings
dominance_rules.trigger: two attributes are about to share one node fill
dominance_rules.action: route one attribute to a separable carrier (border, badge, size)

dominance_rules.rule: Redundant encoding dominates color-only meaning everywhere
dominance_rules.rationale: any color-only distinction fails under CVD, grayscale, and glare
dominance_rules.trigger: color would be the sole carrier of a meaning
dominance_rules.action: add a second channel (shape/position/text/luminance) carrying the same meaning

dominance_rules.rule: Honest quantization dominates a smooth precise-looking ramp for uncertain data
dominance_rules.rationale: a confident continuous color over-claims precision the yield/mastery value lacks
dominance_rules.trigger: a coarse or low-confidence value is about to be rendered as a smooth gradient
dominance_rules.action: quantize into a few bands and mark uncertainty explicitly

dominance_rules.rule: The channel budget dominates the urge to encode one more attribute
dominance_rules.rationale: past a few channels viewers cannot attend the extras and the view degrades to noise
dominance_rules.trigger: an additional attribute is proposed for an already-loaded node
dominance_rules.action: drop, aggregate, or move it into interaction/zoom-in detail rather than adding a channel

dominance_rules.rule: Salience scarcity dominates the wish to flag many conditions
dominance_rules.rationale: popout only works while the flag is rare; proliferation destroys it
dominance_rules.trigger: a second condition wants the red-dot badge
dominance_rules.action: reserve the badge for the single top-priority signal and find another cue for the rest

dominance_rules.rule: A perceptual color space dominates convenient RGB/HSV authoring for any data ramp
dominance_rules.rationale: non-uniform spaces make equal data steps look unequal and mislead
dominance_rules.trigger: a data-encoding ramp is about to be authored in hex/RGB/HSV
dominance_rules.action: specify the ramp in a perceptual space and convert to output at render time

anti_rework_rules.rule: Classify every value's measurement level before assigning any channel
anti_rework_rules.prevents: rebuilding an encoding that put nominal state on an ordered ramp or a magnitude on hue

anti_rework_rules.rule: Choose CVD-safe hues and redundant channels from the start
anti_rework_rules.prevents: re-coloring and re-shaping a whole scheme after it fails colorblind users

anti_rework_rules.rule: Budget the luminance range jointly across intensity, state and contrast up front
anti_rework_rules.prevents: discovering late that bright high-yield nodes break label contrast and re-tuning every band

anti_rework_rules.rule: Decide node channel assignments (fill vs border vs badge) before styling nodes
anti_rework_rules.prevents: tearing apart a fill that blended two integral encodings into one color

anti_rework_rules.rule: Specify all ramps in a perceptual space before picking concrete colors
anti_rework_rules.prevents: re-deriving an uneven RGB ramp whose steps mislead on order

anti_rework_rules.rule: Set the per-node channel budget before adding attributes
anti_rework_rules.prevents: over-encoded nodes that must be stripped back after they read as noise

anti_rework_rules.rule: Reserve the red-dot badge for one signal before wiring flags
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a proliferation of badges that destroys popout and must be pruned

anti_rework_rules.rule: Require a legend whenever color carries meaning
anti_rework_rules.prevents: shipping an undecodable color scheme that must be retrofitted with explanation

iteration_protocol.trigger: the L1 research pass source-verifies (or revises) the Bertin variables, the Cleveland–McGill ranking, CVD prevalence and WCAG ratios
iteration_protocol.action: replace the ESTIMATE-tagged claims with cited FACTs and re-check any encoding that leaned on a revised figure

iteration_protocol.trigger: a CVD simulation confuses two states or two encoded regions
iteration_protocol.action: add or strengthen the redundant channel and re-simulate until the confusion clears

iteration_protocol.trigger: a graph library is chosen for the app and constrains which channels are renderable
iteration_protocol.action: re-map the encodings to the library's supported channels and re-run the channel budget

iteration_protocol.trigger: users are observed reading false precision off an intensity color
iteration_protocol.action: coarsen the quantization and strengthen the uncertainty treatment

iteration_protocol.trigger: the app's dark-theme background luminance changes
iteration_protocol.action: re-check every contrast floor and the luminance budget for intensity and state

iteration_protocol.trigger: a new node attribute or a fourth mastery state must be encoded
iteration_protocol.action: reclassify it and fit it within the channel budget or move it to interaction

iteration_protocol.trigger: the red-dot flag begins carrying more than one condition
iteration_protocol.action: split the extra condition onto a distinct cue and re-verify popout on the single reserved badge

priority_rationale: The encoding frame and the measurement-level taxonomy come first because they decide, for every datum, which channels are even legitimate; the visual variables, the Cleveland–McGill accuracy ranking, preattentive popout and the separable/integral rule follow as the perception science that ranks and constrains those channels; the per-data-type channel prescriptions and the perceptual-color/palette/luminance nodes then turn that science into concrete color machinery; colorblind-safety, redundant encoding and the contrast floor impose the accessibility constraints every color must pass; the app-specific mastery-state, high-yield-intensity, red-dot and multi-channel-composition nodes apply all of it to the actual graph node; and the channel budget, honest-abstraction and color-system verdict come last because they compose every upstream rule into one colorblind-safe, perceptually honest, budget-bounded encoding system with an explicit no-go on color-only meaning, rainbow ramps on ordered data, and false precision.
